stem.text: Ethanal, CH3CHO, reacts with methanol, CH3OH, under acidic conditions to form compound B, as shown in reaction 1.
The initial rate of reaction is investigated using different starting concentrations of CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, CH<sub>3</sub>OH and H<sup>+</sup>. The results obtained are shown in Table 3.1.
Use the information in Table 3.1 to deduce the rate equation for this reaction.
Explain your reasoning. State clearly which experiments you use in your explanation.

guidance: Reasoning must be linked to correct expts – CON once only for M1-M3.
A any correct alternates to M3. –all conditional of orders in M1M2 e.g.
Exp 2 & 4 M3 [CH3CHO] × 2, [CH3OH] × 0.5 and [H+] × 1 / 4 rate × 1 / 4 and so first order to [CH3CHO].
Exp 1 & 3 M3 [CH3CHO] × 0.5, [CH3OH] × 3 and [H+] × 3 rate × 9 / 2 and so first order to [CH3CHO].
Exp 1 & 4 M3 [CH3CHO] × 0.5, [CH3OH] × 3 and [H+] × 4 rate × 6 and so first order to [CH3CHO].

points.text: M1 Exp 1 & 2 [CH3OH] × 1.5 rate × 1.5 or [CH3OH] × 2 / 3 rate × 2 / 3 and so first order to [CH3OH] [1] u / c
M2 Exp 3 & 4 [H+] × 1.33 rate × 1.33 or [H+] × 3 / 4 rate × 3 / 4 and so first order to [H+] [1] u / c
M3 Exp 2 & 3 [CH3CHO] × 0.5, [CH3OH] × 2 and [H+] × 3 rate × 3 and so first order to [CH3CHO] [1] ecf
A second part of M1 M2 M3 ‘and first order’ can be read in from their rate equation
I any annotations on the table unless directed by the candidates

explanation.text: Pick pairs of experiments in which only one concentration changes. Experiments 1 and 2 change only [CH<sub>3</sub>OH] (× 1.5) and the rate also changes × 1.5, so the reaction is first order in CH<sub>3</sub>OH. Experiments 3 and 4 change only [H<sup>+</sup>] (× 4/3) and the rate changes × 4/3, so it is first order in H<sup>+</sup>.

No pair changes [CH3CHO] alone, so use the orders already found. From experiment 2 to 3, [CH3CHO] × 0.5, [CH3OH] × 2 and [H+] × 3. The known first-order terms alone would multiply the rate by 2 × 3 = 6. The rate actually rises only × 3 (3.750 × 10–3 to 1.125 × 10–2), so halving [CH3CHO] halved the rate: first order in CH3CHO. The rate equation is rate = k[CH3OH][H+][CH3CHO], and experiment 1 gives k = 2.500 × 10–3 / (0.500 × 0.040 × 0.100) = 1.25. The order in CH3OH (1) differs from its coefficient in the equation (2): orders come from experiment, not from the balanced equation.

reasoningChain: Exp 1 → 2: only [CH₃OH] changes, × 1.5; rate × 1.5, so first order in CH₃OH.
Exp 3 → 4: only [H⁺] changes, × 4/3; rate × 4/3, so first order in H⁺.
Exp 2 → 3: predicted change from CH₃OH and H⁺ is × 2 × 3 = × 6, actual × 3, so halving [CH₃CHO] halves the rate: first order in CH₃CHO.

inferredMistakes.text: Taking the order in CH₃OH as 2 from the coefficient in the equation for reaction 1.
Comparing two experiments in which several concentrations change, without allowing for the orders already found, and so deducing zero order in CH₃CHO.
Leaving out H⁺ from the rate equation because it is a catalyst.

stem.text: State the units of the rate constant, k, for this reaction.

explanation.text: The reaction is third order overall (1 + 1 + 1). Rearranging rate = k[CH3OH][H+][CH3CHO] gives k = rate / (concentration)3, so the units are (mol dm–3 s–1) / (mol dm–3)3 = mol–2 dm6 s–1.

reasoningChain: k = rate / [ ]³; units = mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ ÷ mol³ dm⁻⁹ = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

inferredMistakes.text: Getting the sign of the dm power wrong, e.g. mol⁻² dm⁻⁶ s⁻¹.

stem.text: Another experiment to investigate reaction 1 is carried out as shown in Table 3.2.
Calculate the initial rate of experiment 5.

guidance: A methods with calculations of k first then rate.

points.text: initial rate = 0.0195 u / c ecf from 3(a)(i) min 2sf

explanation.text: First find k from any experiment in Table 3.1, e.g. experiment 1: k = 2.500 × 10–3 / (0.500 × 0.040 × 0.100) = 1.25 mol–2 dm6 s–1. Then rate = 1.25 × 0.250 × 0.250 × 0.250 = 0.0195 mol dm–3 s–1.

reasoningChain: Calculate k from one experiment in Table 3.1 (k = 1.25).
Substitute the experiment 5 concentrations: rate = 1.25 × 0.250³ = 0.0195 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

inferredMistakes.text: Using the coefficient 2 for CH₃OH from the equation, i.e. squaring [CH₃OH].

stem.text: The reaction of propanone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, with bromine, Br<sub>2</sub>, in the presence of an acid catalyst is shown in reaction 2.
The rate of reaction is first order with respect to [CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>] and first order with respect to [H<sup>+</sup>] under certain conditions.
A three-step mechanism for reaction 2 is suggested.
Complete Table 3.3 to suggest steps 1 and 3 of the mechanism.

stem.caption: Table 3.3
stem.alt: Table 3.3 with three rows. Row 'step 1 (fast)': empty. Row 'step 2 (slow)': protonated propanone, H3C–C(=O+H)–CH3, arrow to the enol H3C–C(OH)=CH2 + H+. Row 'step 3 (fast)': empty.

guidance: I any curly arrows even if incorrect.
markScheme.note: The MS answer is drawn structures for steps 1 and 3 ('each step 2 x [1]'); shown as ms.figure. Points give the same equations as text.

figure.alt: Step 1: propanone H3C–C(=O)–CH3 + H+ arrow to protonated propanone H3C–C(=O+H)–CH3. Step 3: enol H3C–C(OH)=CH2 + Br2 arrow to H3C–C(=O)–CH2Br + HBr.

explanation.text: The rate equation is rate = k[CH3COCH3][H+], so one propanone and one H+ must be involved up to and including the slow step, and Br2 must not be. Step 2 (slow) starts from protonated propanone, so step 1 must make it: propanone + H+ → CH3C(=O+H)CH3. Step 2 forms the enol CH3C(OH)=CH2 and gives back H+. In step 3 (fast, after the slow step, so Br2 does not appear in the rate equation) the enol reacts with Br2 to give CH3COCH2Br + HBr.
Adding the three steps gives back the overall equation for reaction 2, and the H<sup>+</sup> used in step 1 is regenerated in step 2, which is why H<sup>+</sup> is a catalyst.

reasoningChain: Use the rate equation: propanone and H⁺ react before or in the slow step; Br₂ only after it.
Step 1: CH₃COCH₃ + H⁺ → protonated propanone (the reactant of step 2).
Step 3: the enol from step 2 + Br₂ → CH₃COCH₂Br + HBr.
Check the three steps add up to reaction 2 with H⁺ regenerated.

inferredMistakes.text: Putting Br₂ into step 1, which would make the rate depend on [Br₂].
Writing a step 3 product that is still the enol with Br added (e.g. CH₃C(OH)BrCH₂Br) instead of the ketone CH₃COCH₂Br + HBr.

stem.text: Catalysts can be described as homogeneous or heterogeneous.
Describe the mode of action of a heterogeneous catalyst.

guidance: A bullet 1 ‘binds to the surface of the catalyst’ for ‘adsorbed’.

points.text:
(reaction occurs and the) product(s) are desorbed or reaction occurs and substances are desorbed
A product(s) deadsorbed

explanation.text: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase from the reactants, usually a solid with gases or liquids. Its action has three stages: reactant molecules adsorb (form weak bonds) onto active sites on the catalyst surface; this weakens bonds within the reactant molecules, so they react more easily with a lower activation energy; and the products then desorb, leaving the sites free for more reactant. 'Absorb' means taken into the bulk and is not credited.

reasoningChain: Reactants adsorb onto the surface of the catalyst.
Bonds within the reactant molecules are weakened.

inferredMistakes.text: Only saying the catalyst lowers the activation energy, which the MS ignores because it is true of every catalyst and does not describe the heterogeneous mode of action.
